Industrial Policy Resolutions (IFRs) are policy frameworks set by the Indian government to regulate industrial growth, define the role of the public and private sectors, and promote economic development.
First official industrial policy of independent India.
Led by: Dr. Shyama Prasad: Mukherjee (Industry & Commerce Minister). eIt declared the Indian economy as Mixed Economy.
Industries were divided industries into 4 categories:
Strategic Industries (Public Sector): Railways, defense, atomic energy.
Basic/Key Industries (Public-Cum-Private Sector):
Coal, steel, aircraft, telecommunications.
Requiring Regulation (Controlled Private Sector): Sugar, cement, textiles.
Other Industries (Private and Cooperative Sector):
Consumer goods and small-scale industries. eThe start of License Raj > Government control over industries through licensing. elt laid the foundation for public sector dominance in key industries.

The Karve Committee, also known as the Village and Small-Scale Industries Committee, was established by India's Planning Commission in 1955 under the chairmanship of Dattatreya Gopal Karve. It aimed to promote rural industrialization, employment, and balanced economic growth during the Second Five-Year Plan by supporting small-scale industries and local, labour-intensive production.
2nd IPR, 1956 elt also known as the "Economic Constitution of India".
Main Objective of Industrial Policy of 1956 was growth with equity.
It is a framework for socialist industrial growth in India.
Commanding Heights Doctrine (coined by Vladimir Lenin in 1922)
It refers to the state of complete control over the vital industries (such as heavy industries, mining and infrastructure) and it was adopted.
Divided industries into three schedules
Schedule A (17 Industries-Public Sector Monopoly)
> Aviation, Atomic energy, Railways, Arms and Ammunition, Steel and Iron ete.
Schedule B (12 Industries - Public & Private Sectors) > Aluminium, Machine tools, Chemicals etc.
Schedule C (All Other Industries-Private Sector) 3 Consumer goods, Textiles, Automobiles etc.

Classifications of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs)
in India Maharatna Companies (Total-14)
Definition: The highest status, given to large CPSEs with significant global presence.

Criteria: Must have Navratna status, be listed on Indian stock exchanges, and have a 3-year average annual turnover of %25,000+ crore, net worth of %15,000+ crore, and net profit of %5,000+ crore. eThey can invest up to %5,000 crore or 15% of their net worth in a single project without government approval.
Examples: NTPC, BHEL, HAL
Navratna Companies (Total-26)
Definition: Mid-sized CPSEs with competitive advantages.
Criteria: Must be a Miniratna Category I or Schedule A company and have a 'Navratna' score of 60 or more (out of 100)
Autonomy: Can invest up to 31,000 crore or 15% of their net worth without government approval.
Examples: BEL, Engineers India Limited
Miniratna Companies (Total approx.-73)
Definition: Smaller, profitable CPSEs.
Category I: Made profit for the last 3 years consecutively or a pre-tax profit of 30 crore or more in at least one of the three years.
Category II: Made profits for the last 3 years continuously and have a positive net worth.
Examples: Airport Authority of India, Bharat Dynamics Limited 3rd IPR. 1977 (extension of 1956 Policy)

Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR), 1991 — Economic Liberalisation Background The Industrial Policy, 1991 marked a structural shift in India's economy from an inward-looking (closed) system to an outward-oriented (open) economy.
It was introduced under P. V. Narasimha Rao, with reforms led by Dr. Manmohan Singh, during the 1991 Balance of Payments crisis.

Economic Orientation: Before vs After 1991 Before 1991 — Inward-Looking Economy An inward-looking strategy, is a trade and economic policy that prioritizes domestic production over foreign imports to achieve self-reliance. It involves high tariffs, quotas, and subsidies to protect local industries from international competition. It often leads to inefficiencies and lack of innovation.
License Raj (strict government control)
High import barriers (tariffs & quotas)
Import substitution strategy
Result: Low competition, inefficiency, slow growth 1991 Reforms — Transition (LPG Model)
Liberalisation: Refers to the reduction of government regulations, licenses, and restrictions on industrial growth and international trade, thereby freeing up markets.
Privatisation: Involves shifting ownership or management of government-owned enterprises (public sector units) to private entities, enhancing efficiency/competitiveness and reducing state burden.

To implement the privatization objective of the 1991 LPG reforms, the government later established DIPAM (Department of Investment and Public Asset Management, earlier known as the Department of Disinvestment) under the Ministry of Finance to manage disinvestment and reduce government ownership in Public Sector Enterprises.
Minority Disinvestment: The government retains a majority stake (usually > 51%) and management control, selling only a small portion to public/institutional investors.
Majority Disinvestment: The government reduces its stake below 51%,giving majority control to private or other entities.
Strategic Disinvestment: The sale of a substantial portion of government shareholding (often 50% or more) along with the transfer of management control to a private entity.
Complete Privatization (Full Exit): A type of strategic sale where the government sells 100% of its equity, fully exiting the enterprise.
Globalisation: Integrates the national economy with the global economy through increased trade, foreign investment (FDI), and free movement of goods and technology across borders Key Measures
End of License Raj (except few industries)
FDI liberalisation (automatic route)
Reduction in public sector monopoly
Greater role of market forces
Important Macroeconomic Reforms

Fiscal Deficit (1990-91): ~10% of GDP
Anti-Dumping Duty: Protects domestic industries
HDFC Bank - First private sector bank after liberalisation After 1991 — Outward-Oriented Economy Outcomes:
Increase in FDI inflows (major benefit of FDI for developing countries like India - Access to technology and employment).
Growth of private sector
Rise in competition and efficiency. eIndia moved from Import Substitution Industrialization.
e (ISI) to Export-Oriented Industrialization (EOI)
Global economic integration.
Flow of capital, technology, and services. eEmergence of BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) sector.
India adopted Managed floating exchange rate.
Structural Changes in Economy:
India's service sector became the primary driver of GDP, with its share rising from around 39% in 1991-92 to over 55-60% in recent years.
Share of agriculture in India's GDP has experienced a steady, long-term decline, dropping from nearly 30% in 1990-91 to around 15-18% in recent years.
Manufacturing sector share in GDP has largely stagnated.
Joint Sector refers to a form of partnership between the public sector (government) and the private sector.
Dutta Committee (1973) recommended the establishment of Joint Venture Sector in Indian Industry.
